mainEntity.name: Can a dentist put a crown on a tooth that is mostly gum?

acceptedAnswer.text: This depends on what lies beneath the gumline. If the root is healthy, intact, and of sufficient length, techniques such as crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion may expose more tooth structure, making crown placement more feasible. However, if the tooth is fractured below the bone or the root is compromised, extraction and tooth replacement may be more appropriate. This can only be determined through a clinical examination, which typically includes dental X-rays.

mainEntity.name: What is a post and core, and how does it help save a tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: A post and core is a two-part dental restoration used when a tooth lacks sufficient structure to retain a crown on its own. A post — usually made from metal or fibre — is inserted into the root canal and cemented in place. A core of filling material is then built up around this post, recreating the shape needed to support a crown. It is important to note that the post retains the core rather than strengthening the root itself.

mainEntity.name: How long does a crown last on a heavily restored tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crown longevity varies considerably depending on the individual tooth, the quality of the remaining foundation, the materials used, and how well the patient maintains their oral hygiene. In general, dental crowns can last many years when placed on a stable and well-prepared foundation. However, teeth with minimal remaining structure or those without an adequate ferrule may be at greater risk of complications over time. Your dentist can discuss realistic expectations based on your specific situation.

mainEntity.name: Is crown lengthening a painful procedure?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crown lengthening is typically performed under local anaesthetic, so patients should not experience pain during the procedure itself. Some tenderness and mild swelling in the days following surgery is normal and usually manageable with over-the-counter pain relief as advised by your dental team. The healing period before a crown can be fitted usually takes several weeks, allowing the gum and bone to fully stabilise.

mainEntity.name: What happens if a tooth cannot support a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: If a tooth cannot safely or predictably support a crown — for example, if the root is fractured, too short, or compromised by infection — extraction may be the most clinically appropriate option. Following extraction, there are several ways to restore the space, including dental implants, fixed bridges, or partial dentures. Your dentist will discuss all relevant options with you based on a thorough assessment of your oral health.

mainEntity.name: Will I lose the tooth if there is very little of it left above the gum?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Many teeth with minimal visible structure above the gumline can still be saved with the right clinical approach, provided the root is healthy and adequate bone support remains. However, this is always an individual decision based on clinical findings. In some cases, attempting to retain a heavily compromised tooth may not offer a predictable long-term outcome, and a discussion about tooth replacement may be the most honest and patient-centred course of action.
